rationale: H2 is directly detected in the plume; CO2 is part of the inferred ocean/carbonate system; CH4 is detected. Enceladus-specific modelling and laboratory experiments support methanogenesis as chemically plausible. Abiotic CH4 remains a major confounder, so the pathway is strong as a hypothesis but not diagnostic by itself.

ThermoBase contains substantial sulfate-reduction diversity, but the Enceladus case is less directly constrained than methanogenesis by the currently emphasized H2/CH4 observations. A future sulfur-speciation measurement would be more discriminating.

ThermoBase contains extensive sulfur-reducing thermophiles. However, elemental sulfur and biologically diagnostic sulfide production are not constrained at the same evidentiary level as H2 and CH4 in the present case.
ThermoBase contains explicit Fe(III)-reducing organisms, but the Enceladus case lacks an equivalently strong observational constraint on bioavailable Fe(III) as an electron acceptor.

reaction: Representative reduced-carbon oxidation by an external oxidant
rationale: Oxidant-driven metabolisms are biologically plausible and ThermoBase contains many examples, but the relevant oxidant inventories remain less directly constrained than plume H2.
